extracted.intended_audience: scientists who serve as peer reviewers and researchers interested in NIH grant review and funding policy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and commentary on behaviors, procedures, and policy choices that shape peer review of manuscripts and NIH grant applications (reviewer conduct, journal/CSR notification practices, study-section clustering, two-stage reviews). Aimed at people who read/serve on study sections and follow NIH review policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read other reviewers' comments
rubrics_metrics.description: You should always read over the comments of the other reviewers as a continuing education / calibration of your own reviewing behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading colleagues' critiques helps calibrate your evaluations and is part of reviewer continuing education. The blog emphasizes this as a routine professional practice reviewers should follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include reviews with decision notifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should send the Editor Decision and reviews together in the notification instead of only emailing the decision and requiring the reviewer to log into the site to see other reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consolidating decision + reviews in the notification reduces friction and increases the number of reviewers who will read other reviewers' comments. 'Easy. Peasy.' — the post argues this is a simple change journals can make.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize reviewer-site friction for accessing reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring the reviewer to go back and log into the reviewer site and make a few clicks decreases the numbers who are going to read over the other reviewer comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design reviewer notification/UI workflows to minimize extra login/click burdens; lower friction increases engagement with peer feedback and calibration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid clustering / 'OldBoy' cronyism in funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Breaking up OldBoy type cronyism is a good goal — clustering/insular sub-groupings of scientists can protect and maintain themselves and their peers through the grant review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses of funded grant outputs and study-section behavior (e.g., CRISP/IFCN clustering) can detect clustering. The post argues funding policies and review practices should aim to reduce insular protection to preserve fairness and scientific diversity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-stage/mail-in reviewers focus on design and methods (not impact)
rubrics_metrics.description: College reviewers primarily will provide written or 'mail-in' critiques and be involved in two-stage reviews; initial reviewers will be expected to nitpick the design and methods, with talk of impact and significance for regular review rolled back.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that different reviewer roles may have distinct evaluation emphases: mail-in/second-stage reviewers may be asked to concentrate on technical rigor and methodology rather than broader impact statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use two-stage reviews for special application sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Two-stage reviews have successfully assessed thousands of special sets of applications, such as the Transformative R01 and Challenge grant applications as well as groups of translational applications and small business applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider two-stage/review structures when assessing unusual, high-risk/high-reward, translational, or clustered application types; this structure may be suitable for targeted program announcements and challenge grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for study design limitations when evaluating evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary analyses based on survey data are correlational in nature, not prospective experiments; interpreters and reviewers should recognize these limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating research claims (e.g., effects of anti-drug messages), explicitly note whether the design is correlational vs experimental and avoid overinterpreting causal claims from correlational analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor reviewer feedback when implementing review changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Feedback from those who sat on the second stage of the Transformative and Challenge reviews this summer sure wasn’t all that positive — reviewer experience should inform whether changes are successful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before and after rolling out major review-policy changes (new reviewer pools, two-stage reviews, college reviewers), collect and weigh reviewer feedback and experiences; negative feedback should prompt re-evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase reviewer inclusion by offering remote/mail-in participation
rubrics_metrics.description: CSR is sending invitations to about 2,500 members of the scientific community to join a 'College of Reviewers' to allow reviewers who find it difficult to manage travel and commitment of regular reviewing to remain engaged via written/mail-in critiques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expand reviewer pools by enabling mail-in and remote participation to retain reviewers who cannot travel; balance inclusion with maintaining review quality and role clarity.
